source: Algorithmically extracted from world/data/source/floor-14-plan-hires.png (2026-08-02 re-extraction against the hi-res source). floor-14-plan-hires.png (636x489) is the actual image published in Northeastern's GSE Vancouver handbook PDF, page 14 -- the authoritative original of the same drawing every prior pass traced from a 473x364 screenshot of. Same drawing, 1.8x the pixels, no screenshot resampling. Pipeline unchanged in kind from the prior pass (OpenCV intensity threshold at 180 isolates dark wall ink from light-grey furniture; connected-component filtering by bbox long-side, fill density, text-row height and corner-logo position strips specks/icons/labels/the N logo; HoughLinesP fragments are clustered by (angle, perpendicular offset) and merged via total-least-squares/PCA line fitting; gaps <=3.5px bridged as antialiasing noise, any other gap left as a real door opening), with every size-dependent constant retuned for this resolution (~1.33x the old pixel density) and two fixes specific to this pass: (1) two tight boxes over the upper core's physical stairwell drop antialiasing-noise fragments that happened to read as axis-aligned and slip past the existing diagonal-decoration filter (the X-shaft icons and stair hatching are still dropped by angle, 15-75 degrees off axis-aligned, exactly as before); (2) any merged wall segment lying entirely inside a hole polygon (all three probe points -- both endpoints and the midpoint, with a 0.05m radius absorbing the sub-cm rounding on dividers whose tip touches the hole's own boundary line by construction) is dropped, since the walls-only scorer's own target already excludes ink strictly inside the core holes, so drawing that internal shaft/stair detail is pure precision risk for zero recall upside -- the hole polygon's own boundary already carries the outer silhouette. Result improves the wall-match score against the hi-res reference on both axes: walls-only precision 84.7%->92.2%, recall 90.8%->95.6%, F1 87.7%->93.9%; all-structural-ink precision 95.5%->97.2%, recall 78.2%->79.4%, F1 86.0%->87.4%.
note: Transform: world_x = (px - x0) * s, world_z = (bh - (py - y0)) * s -- ONE uniform scale s = 0.055644 m/px applied to every point, after shifting pixel coordinates so the building's own wall-network bounding box (the outer envelope + every partition wall that touches it, all one pixel-connected component in this line drawing; 629x471px at (0,1) in the trimmed-canvas frame) starts at (0,0); s is calibrated so the building's long (x) axis is 35.0m. Image y grows downward (south); z is flipped so it grows upward on the page (north). No bbox-nudge hack (unlike the old 473x364 pipeline, whose trimmed canvas was a few px bigger than the building's own footprint because its trim also caught the north-arrow/logo graphic): the hi-res source is full-bleed against its own canvas with no such margin, and after excluding the logo/title-block by connected-component position (not by cropping) the building's own bounding box already reproduces the source's aspect almost exactly with a plain uniform scale (aspect 1.333 vs the scorer's own 629x471px reference bbox, 1.335). The outline is the external contour of that same outer-envelope component; the two elevator/stair core holes are the external contours of the two free-standing core-band components (the lower one clipped to a measured pixel row -- the shaft row's own bottom rail, confirmed by direct zoom against the source to be one continuous straight line with no notches, unlike the upper band -- so the Female/Male/Gender-Neutral washroom partitions hanging off its south edge are not swallowed into the hole; a real gap separates the two holes, so the corridor between them stays walkable). Room centers/doors are carried over byte-for-byte from the prior (473px-source) file: they were hand-matched to each room's real label/doorway position, only need to land inside the right room near its real threshold (a far looser bar than wall tracing), and the building has not moved between source images -- verified by overlay and by `npm run test:nav` (18/18 rooms path-reachable) after the swap. The 8 glass:true walls (was 5) are the same design judgment as the prior file -- the source line drawing has no glass/solid notation anywhere, so this is a documented choice, not a surveyed fact -- carried forward onto their hi-res equivalents by endpoint-position matching rather than re-derived from scratch; the hi-res source resolves the Kitchen/1407/1408-vs-Event-Space front as more (shorter, jogged) segments than the old low-res screenshot's Hough merge could resolve, so more individual wall entries now carry that one continuous design decision (see each glass wall's own `note` field for specifics). Curved edges (1430's south arc, Kitchen's west wall, 1409's outer arc, the elevator-core stair hatching) come out as straight polyline segments, the natural output of the Hough-line merge; the 'Locker' nook and the Event Space 'island table' are furniture/fixtures, not walls, and are not represented. Washroom partition walls use height 2.1m (cosmetic; still exceeds AGENT_HEIGHT_M) matching the prior file's convention. `walls[]` entries are NOT render-only. CORRECTED 2026-08-02: an earlier version of this note claimed they were, saying the navmesh came from `walkableOutline` + `holes` alone. That is FALSE. `world/src/nav/buildNavMesh.ts` extrudes EVERY `walls[]` entry into a vertical quad that becomes a real Recast obstacle (see `buildGeometry`, which calls `addWallQuad` for every wall). Walls are load-bearing NAVIGATION geometry as well as render geometry (world-client Walls.tsx). This matters: a room whose walls form a fully closed loop becomes a disconnected navmesh island and is unreachable no matter what its `door` coordinate says, which is exactly what happened to the Gender Neutral Washroom during this hi-res re-trace, and the false note is part of why it was hard to spot. If you add, move or trim a wall, re-run `cd world && npm run test:nav`: it asserts every room door is reachable AND that Detour did not silently return a PARTIAL path. Geometry REBUILD pass (world/data/tools/rebuild_floor_plan.py): the walls array is no longer the raster trace's own segment list; it is constructed from clean primitives. Both elevator/stair core polygons are simple, correctly wound axis-aligned rectangles over their own bands, matching the two plain horizontal core bands the source drawing shows; the upper one came out of the trace as a self-intersecting 29-point polygon, which is what had let the shaft boxes inside it survive as walls and render as a comb across the middle of the floor. 20 walls are one-per-edge of walkableOutline (a closed envelope by construction), 8 are one-per-edge of the two repaired elevator/stair core polygons, and 56 are interior partitions admitted from the trace: a traced segment is kept only if it is at least 0.5 m long, its midpoint is outside both core polygons, and it does not shadow an envelope or core wall (within 8 degrees and 0.45 m with real overlap). Admitted partitions were then merged where collinear, welded at ends within 0.20 m, and landed on the perpendicular foot of any wall body within 0.50 m, with the envelope and core pinned so they keep matching walkableOutline and the holes exactly. Any partition end still stopping in open space afterwards, with no neighbour to land on and no door facing it, was then decided against the source raster in source/floor-14-plan-hires.png: an end whose own axis reaches a neighbour within 0.90 m is landed on it, a run the trace chopped is bridged, and an end is only ever closed where every point of the added span sits within 0.15 m of drawn ink, which is what distinguishes a joint the trace lost from a door opening the drawing leaves blank (measured on this plan: real wall bodies run 0.05 to 0.12 m from ink, the door openings 0.36 to 0.47 m). Ink is greyscale below 150, not below 130 as in earlier passes: this drawing renders its thin interior partitions in LIGHT grey around 133 to 140 (sampled down the washroom block's right wall and the Gender Neutral washroom's left wall), so at 130 those walls read as blank paper and every break the trace left in them was preserved as if it were a doorway. Genuinely blank paper on this drawing is 200 and above, so the two populations are still cleanly separated. Two further passes then run on the corrected reading. The first judges a PAIR of loose ends rather than one end at a time and closes the gap between them when a third wall runs straight through it (a junction the drawing interrupts, which is why the washroom block's south wall stops at both faces of the plumbing chase between the Male and Female washrooms) or when the span is on ink once these two walls' OWN tracing error is allowed for (the Classroom 1417 / North Collaboration run is traced about 0.2 m off its own drawn line along its whole length, so a flat bound calls the joint between its two pieces blank for the same reason it would call the pieces themselves blank). The second emits wall the drawing has and the trace has none of at all, found by reading along a loose end's own axis past a blank opening: the washroom block's right wall below the Gender Neutral washroom's door, and the 1429/1430 jamb. A run only counts if it is a LINE with paper 0.28 m to either side, which is what keeps the washroom pictograms and the heavy room labels from being read as walls. 1 end remains loose by design, each one a jamb facing an opening the drawing shows as a blank gap. Wall dimensions and angles are therefore constructed, not surveyed. No weld or snap was allowed to narrow a door-sized opening, and every room stays path-reachable (npm run test:nav, 18/18, no PARTIAL paths); glass flags and authored per-wall notes are carried onto the nearest parallel rebuilt wall. Finally, no wall here is a shadow stub: a tab under 0.80 m with a free end lying flat against a longer wall (within 25 degrees and 0.25 m, its shadow inside that wall's span) is not kept as a wall of its own, because the line is already drawn by the wall it shadows and the tab renders as a spur poking past the junction. Its glass flag and its authored note move onto that wall first, paragraph by paragraph, so the design decision survives at the same place on the front; a short wall joining two others is never absorbed, since deleting one of those would strand its neighbour. Two further passes then judge a wall's whole BODY against the drawing rather than its ends, which is what every pass above looks at. The first moves a partition that runs parallel BESIDE the line it represents onto that line: ON INK means drawn ink within 0.09 m of the wall's centreline, half its rendered thickness, and a wall covering less than 0.60 of its own length is refitted by a search over the perpendicular offset of each END (so a wall traced across its line, like Classroom 1417's north front at -0.33 m one end and +0.39 m the other, is straightened as well as shifted), capped at 12 degrees of turn and only where the fit gains 0.20 of coverage and moves at least 0.15 m. A wall with a drawn line down BOTH sides of it for at least 0.80 of its length is left exactly where it is: that is a wall the drawing renders as its two faces (the 0.72 m plumbing chase between the Male and Female washrooms scores 0.99 on both sides) and the centreline between them is already the right answer, the same answer the bundle fusion above reaches. Junctions the refit moved are re-formed at the centroid of their moved ends, and the regularizer runs again so neighbours follow. The second restores the ARCS the trace flattened into single straight chords (the Kitchen's west glass wall, 1430's south edge, 1408's front against Event Space). An arc is measured as a SAGITTA, how far the drawn line bows off the chord at mid-span against the straight line between the ink at its two ends; at or past 0.10 m, two thirds of the rendered wall thickness, the drawn line has left the wall that is supposed to be drawing it, and the chord is replaced by a 3 to 6 segment polyline whose interior vertices sit on the ink. Both endpoints are kept exactly, so whatever was attached at either end stays attached, and `glass` and any authored note ride onto every piece, because each piece IS that wall. An arc in walls[] is therefore DERIVED, not stored: every run starts by collapsing each polyline back into the one chord it was built from (recognised by re-curving that chord and matching the result piece for piece) and re-derives it at the end, so the file is a fixpoint rather than a curve that gets re-cut on every pass. One last pass then asks a question none of the above asks: not what the drawing shows, but whether the simulation can WALK through it. world/src/nav/agentProfile.ts erodes the navmesh by AGENT_RADIUS_M = 0.20 on both sides of every wall, so a traced 0.63 m doorway leaves 0.23 m of walkable corridor, narrower than the 0.40 m agent itself, and visitors queue at the door instead of going through it. Every opening under 1.20 m is therefore widened to it by pulling its jambs BACK ALONG THEIR OWN LINES, balanced about the opening, so a doorway grows without any wall leaving its line or changing its bearing; 1.20 m leaves 0.80 m walkable, two whole agent diameters, which is what lets two agents pass in opposite directions. These openings are therefore WIDER than the source drawing's, deliberately: this is a simulation floor, not a construction document. The pass only ever REMOVES material, so it cannot contradict the door guardrails above (all of which forbid ADDING material near an opening) and a room's door anchor can only come out further from the nearest wall than it went in. It will not trim a jamb below 0.455 m (the admission floor above, plus a rounding margin, so a widened jamb is never deleted on the next run instead of shortened), past a point where another wall T-joins its body, or nearer than 0.25 m to a neighbouring endpoint the weld above would then drag it onto; and it never trims the envelope or the core at all. Where those floors bind, the opening is widened as far as is safe and left short rather than forced, which is why the washroom block's east wall keeps two narrow doors: 3.03 m of wall line cannot hold three jambs and two full width openings, and the widening will not delete a jamb to pretend otherwise. Wall glass flags were auto-classified as a FIRST PASS by world/data/tools/classify_glass.py (a wall is glass when it separates an enclosed room from an open/public area, solid between two enclosed rooms, and solid for every Kitchen wall, the cores, and any no-door space), intended for manual refinement in the interactive editor. Glass flags set by hand via the interactive glass-marker tool (user selection), superseding the auto-classification first pass.
